newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Allied Domecq taskforce to study merger.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Allied Domecq taskforce to study merger.

text.p: British drinks group Allied Domecq said on Tuesday it was studying whether a planned merger between rivals Grand Metropolitan Plc and Guinness gives them an unfair dominance in any of its markets.
"We have set up a taskforce to look at the issue," Allied chairman Sir Christopher Hogg said in an interview.
Hogg, however, was optimistic about the prospects for his company after the mega-merger.

"I think we are in a very good position following yesterday's merger, we have 12 of the top 100 brands, we are in increasingly good shape in wines and spirits and we can seize oppurtunities open to us which will be greatly increased by the merger," he said.
Allied shares were 19.5 pence higher at 466p in mid-afternoon as investors took a view that the group was now more vulnerable to a takeover in the wake of its rivals' merger.
Some investors believe the merger leaves Allied looking weak and in dire need of strategic partners if it is to stop its market share being eroded.
Hogg said it was far too early to say whether Allied would complain to monopoly authorities about the planned merger. "There is so much to be examined and analysed."
"We have to look at it on a market by market, territory by territory basis. But we have a duty to complain if it's in shareholders interests," he said.

Earlier Allied announced first half results which showed a one percent fall in pretax profits at actual exchange rates to 317 million pounds ($514.5 million), with profits from its spirits and wine division down two percent at 239 million pounds.

"We believe this weak result in spirits really brings Allied to the table," said SocGen analyst Nick Lyall. "The spirits business is struggling but you have to be aware of the takeover speculation now in play."

The proposed 24 billion pound Guinness/Grand Met merger, announced on Monday, creates the world's seventh largest branded food and drinks company, GMG Brands. It will be the leading spirits and wine group with combined annual sales of more than 100 million cases.
Subject to European Union and U.S. regulatory approval, the merger would create a combined spirits division controlling half the Scotch whisky business worldwide.

However, both joint chairmen of GMG Brands said on Monday they did not anticipate any problems from competition authorities, although Canadian-based Seagram the world's second largest spirits company, described the deal anti-competitive.

Spain and the United States are expected to be the most sensitive markets for Allied if the merger is allowed to go ahead without regulatory controls. In the U.S. GrandMet is the largest spirits company and Guinness the largest whisky group.
Spain is Allied's largest European market, the group sold some two million cases of Ballantine's whisky there last year and half a million cases of Beefeater gin.

Spain and the United States together generate half of Allied's profits in its spirits and wine division. In Spain, GrandMet-owned J&B is the largest Scotch brand and Guinness sells Johnnie Walker whisky and Gordon's gin.

Earlier Hogg told reporters however that he did not want the companies "response to be one of complaint," and he talked in positive terms about consolidation in the industry as a force for improving growth.
"Spirits is a tough industry in which to get growth and anything which is likely to improve growth is going to be looked at seriously," he told reporters.
"Consolidation does afford oppurtunities to grow profits whether from increased marketing power or reduced costs."
"Consolidation is one way forward for the industry."

If Allied had demerged its spirits division, as some shareholders called for a year ago, it would have meant a 15 month programme and a good deal of turmoil, leaving it less able to take advantage of any fall out from the GrandMet/Guinness merger, said Hogg.

"I think we are in a very good position following yesterday's merger, we have 12 of the top 100 brands, we are in increasingly good shape in wines and spirits and we can seize oppurtunities open to us which will be greatly increased by the merger," said Hogg.
The company said it expects its second half results to benefit from favourable spirits shipments to the United States and higher first half investment in its pubs.

Sales of spirits in continental Europe were down three percent in the first half and in America one percent lower. Volume increases in Spain and Germany were offset by declines in volume in Britain, Greece and Italy.

In Britain Teacher's whisky lost volume in the face of tougher pricing by competitors but sales of Courvoisier brandy improved. The company continued to concentrate its marketing effort on four core brands -- Ballantine's, Beefeater, Kahlua liqueur and Mexican drink Sauza.

Trading profit from the group's retailing division fell one percent to 105 million pounds with growth in its managed pubs like Big Steak Pubs and Firkin being offset by lower profits from off-licence chain Victoria Wine. ($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
